Structural identification: from Cholesky to proxies and sign restrictions

Source: vignettes/identification.Rmd
identification.Rmd

1. The identification problem

The reduced-form VAR delivers innovations utu_t with covariance Σ\Sigma. A structural VAR posits ut=Pεtu_t=P\varepsilon_t with orthonormal shocks, E[εtεt′]=IKE[\varepsilon_t\varepsilon_t']=I_K, which requires PP′=ΣPP'=\Sigma. Any such PP can be written P=P̃QP=\tilde P Q where P̃=chol(Σ)\tilde P=\mathrm{chol}(\Sigma) and QQ is an orthogonal matrix (QQ′=IQQ'=I). The data pin down Σ\Sigma, hence P̃\tilde P, but say nothing about QQ: there are K(K−1)/2K(K-1)/2 free parameters, and different QQ give observationally equivalent models with different impulse responses Θh=ΦhP\Theta_h=\Phi_h P. An identification scheme is a set of assumptions that selects QQ (point identification) or restricts it to a set (set identification). Each id_*() constructor in varm returns such a scheme and is passed as the id argument of irf(), fevd() and hd(), for both varm (frequentist) and bvarm (Bayesian) fits. Results are drawn with autoplot() (ggplot2) and tabulated with tidy(), whose columns are response, shock, horizon, estimate and, when bands exist, level, conf.low, conf.high.

constructor assumption identification
id_chol(order) recursive: PP lower triangular after ordering point
id_longrun() long-run multiplier lower triangular (Blanchard-Quah) point
id_restrictions(impact, longrun) arbitrary zero pattern on PP and/or Θ(1)\Theta(1) (A-B / mixed) point (just-identified)
id_sign(restrictions, ...) signs of IRFs over some horizons set
id_zerosign(sign, zero, zero_lr, ...) zeros and signs (ARRW) set (weights not implemented)
id_proxy(z, fit) / proxy_draws() external instrument for one shock point, one shock
id_hetero(fit, regime) two variance regimes (Rigobon) point, statistical shocks
id_given(P) user supplied impact matrix point

1.1 The A/B model, counting and observational equivalence

The general structural form (Amisano and Giannini, 1997; Luetkepohl, 2005, ch. 9) is Aut=Bεt,εt∼(0,IK), A\,u_t = B\,\varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t\sim(0,I_K), so that Σ=A−1BB′A−1′\Sigma = A^{-1}BB'A^{-1\prime} and the impact matrix is P=A−1BP=A^{-1}B. Three special cases cover most practice: the A-model (B=IB=I, so Aut=εtAu_t=\varepsilon_t, structural shocks with unit variance after normalising the diagonal of AA), the B-model (A=IA=I, ut=Bεtu_t=B\varepsilon_t, which is the form used by varm) and the AB-model. Σ\Sigma has K(K+1)/2K(K+1)/2 distinct elements, while PP has K2K^2, so a necessary order condition is that the restrictions supply at least K2−K(K+1)2=K(K−1)2 K^2-\frac{K(K+1)}{2}=\frac{K(K-1)}{2} independent restrictions. For K=3K=3 that is three. The condition is not sufficient (Rubio-Ramirez, Waggoner and Zha, 2010 give the exact rank condition for zeros): PP is identified up to the sign of each column, i.e. up to the 2K2^K matrices PDPD with DD diagonal ±1\pm1. This sign indeterminacy is resolved by a normalisation, which is a convention and not an identifying assumption, but it changes what “a positive shock” means.

Observational equivalence. If PP and P̃=PQ\tilde P=PQ with QQ′=IQQ'=I both satisfy PP′=ΣPP'=\Sigma, the likelihood, the forecasts and the reduced-form IRFs coincide; only the structural IRFs ΦhP\Phi_hP and the labels of the shocks differ. Identification restrictions are therefore untestable in the just-identified case, and only over-identifying restrictions leave a testable implication. In varm, over-identification is rejected by id_restrictions().

Pc <- t(chol(fit$Sigma))                              # one admissible P
th <- 0.7; Q <- matrix(c(cos(th), sin(th), 0, -sin(th), cos(th), 0, 0, 0, 1), 3)   # a rotation in the (1,2) plane
Pq <- Pc %*% Q
c(`PP' = Sigma for chol` = max(abs(Pc %*% t(Pc) - fit$Sigma)),
  `PP' = Sigma for rotated` = max(abs(Pq %*% t(Pq) - fit$Sigma)))
#>    PP' = Sigma for chol PP' = Sigma for rotated 
#>            1.387779e-17            2.775558e-17
round(cbind(chol_col1 = Pc[, 1], rotated_col1 = Pq[, 1]), 3)   # same fit, different "first shock"
#>       chol_col1 rotated_col1
#> infl      0.308        0.235
#> unemp    -0.012        0.205
#> rate      0.088       -0.106

Both matrices reproduce Σ\Sigma to machine precision, yet they imply different first shocks. Everything that follows is a way of choosing QQ (equivalently, PP).

2. Cholesky (recursive) identification

Definition. Order the variables (y1,…,yK)(y_1,\dots,y_K). Take P=chol(Σ)P=\mathrm{chol}(\Sigma) (lower triangular, positive diagonal). Then shock jj affects variables j,…,Kj,\dots,K on impact but not variables 1,…,j−11,\dots,j-1: variable ii responds contemporaneously only to shocks 1,…,i1,\dots,i. The restriction is K(K−1)/2K(K-1)/2 zeros in PP, which exactly identifies the model.

Economic story (monetary policy). Order infl, unemp, rate (the column order of yraw). The assumption is that prices and unemployment are predetermined within the quarter with respect to monetary policy (they are sticky and do not react to a policy surprise in the same quarter), while the central bank sets the rate after seeing current inflation and unemployment. The last shock is then the monetary-policy shock. This is the classic recursive scheme of Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (1999).

ir1 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 20, ci = "wild", nboot = 300)
round(ir1$estimate[, , 1], 3)   # impact matrix P (rows: response, columns: shock): lower triangular
#>         shock
#> response   infl  unemp  rate
#>    infl   0.308  0.000 0.000
#>    unemp -0.012  0.332 0.000
#>    rate   0.088 -0.268 0.715
autoplot(ir1, shocks = rate)

A one-standard-deviation policy shock raises the rate by about 0.7 percentage points on impact. The path of inflation after the shock is the usual diagnostic: a significantly positive response (the “price puzzle”) signals that the recursive scheme or the information set is misspecified: the VAR does not contain what the central bank knows (for instance commodity prices or forecasts) and the “shock” is partly an anticipated reaction to inflation.

Ordering matters. Only the variable ordering, not the choice of recursive PP given an ordering, is a modelling decision. Moving rate first says the policy rate is exogenous within the quarter, which is not a monetary-policy shock at all. Comparing orderings is a cheap robustness check:

ir2 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(order = c(rate, infl, unemp)), horizon = 20, ci = "none")
round(ir2$estimate[, "rate", 1], 3)   # impact responses to the "rate" shock when rate is ordered first
#>   infl  unemp   rate 
#>  0.035 -0.117  0.769
# ribbon and solid line: rate last; dashed: rate first
autoplot(ir1, shocks = rate) +
  geom_line(data = subset(tidy(ir2), shock == "rate"), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20")

The residual correlation (cor(resid(fit))) tells you how much the ordering can matter: with correlations near zero all orderings agree. Here the rate and unemployment residuals have a correlation of about −0.35-0.35, so the order matters for those two.

All orderings. With K=3K=3 there are six orderings. The response of inflation at h=4h=4 to the shock attached to the policy rate (the shock labelled rate in the output, whichever position it takes in the recursion) shows how much the answer depends on the assumption:

nm <- colnames(yraw)
perms <- list(c(1, 2, 3), c(1, 3, 2), c(2, 1, 3), c(2, 3, 1), c(3, 1, 2), c(3, 2, 1))
tab <- t(sapply(perms, function(o) {
  e <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(order = all_of(nm[o])), horizon = 4, ci = "none")$estimate
  c(rate_shock_on_inflation_h4 = e["infl", "rate", 5], rate_shock_on_rate_h0 = e["rate", "rate", 1])
}))
rownames(tab) <- sapply(perms, function(o) paste(substr(nm[o], 1, 3), collapse = ">"))
round(tab, 3)
#>             rate_shock_on_inflation_h4 rate_shock_on_rate_h0
#> inf>une>rat                     -0.058                 0.715
#> inf>rat>une                      0.038                 0.764
#> une>inf>rat                     -0.058                 0.715
#> une>rat>inf                      0.007                 0.719
#> rat>inf>une                      0.106                 0.769
#> rat>une>inf                      0.106                 0.769

Only orderings that put rate last give the policy-shock interpretation of section 2; the others show the range of what other timing assumptions would imply. Cholesky orderings are observationally equivalent in fit, so the data cannot choose among them.

Normalisation: one standard deviation vs unit shocks

With PP′=ΣPP'=\Sigma shocks have unit variance, so responses are to a one-standard-deviation shock. Policy discussions usually want a fixed size shock, such as 25 basis points. irf(normalise = normalise_to(shock, variable, size)) rescales the shock so that the impact response of variable equals size (draw by draw, so the bands reflect the rescaling too).

irn <- irf(fit, horizon = 20, ci = "wild", nboot = 300,
           normalise = normalise_to(rate, rate, 0.25))
round(irn$estimate["rate", "rate", 1], 3)           # impact response is exactly 0.25
#> [1] 0.25
round(irn$estimate[, "rate", c(1, 5, 9, 13)], 3)
#>         h
#> response    0      4      8     12
#>    infl  0.00 -0.020 -0.027 -0.031
#>    unemp 0.00  0.014  0.026  0.020
#>    rate  0.25  0.135  0.076  0.046

The normalisation changes only the scale of the responses for point identified schemes (all of them scale linearly), but for ratios across variables it avoids a classic pitfall: comparing responses in “standard-deviation units” across models whose shock variances differ.

3. Long-run restrictions (Blanchard-Quah)

Definition. Let F=I−∑lAlF=I-\sum_l A_l. The long-run (cumulative) multiplier of the structural shocks is Θ(1)=∑h=0∞Θh=F−1P. \Theta(1)=\sum_{h=0}^\infty \Theta_h=F^{-1}P . Blanchard and Quah (1989) impose that Θ(1)\Theta(1) is lower triangular: shock jj has no permanent effect on variables 1,…,j−11,\dots,j-1. varm computes Θ(1)Θ(1)′=F−1ΣF−1′\Theta(1)\Theta(1)'=F^{-1}\Sigma F^{-1\prime}, takes its Cholesky factor LL, and sets P=FLP=FL. The order of the variables is the column order of the data.

Economic story (supply and demand). In the original application yt=(ΔGDPt,unemploymentt)′y_t=(\Delta \text{GDP}_t,\ \text{unemployment}_t)', the first shock is “supply” (the only shock with a permanent effect on output) and the second is “demand” (transitory by assumption). Variables must be stationary (growth rates or differences) for the long-run matrix to be meaningful. yraw has no output series, so we illustrate the mechanics with yt=(Δπt,ut)′y_t=(\Delta \pi_t,\ u_t)': the first shock is the only one that can permanently change the level of inflation (a “nominal trend” shock) and the second is transitory for inflation.

d2 <- data.frame(dinfl = diff(yraw$infl), unemp = yraw$unemp[-1])
f2 <- varm(d2, p = 2)
round(max(stability(f2)), 3)
#> [1] 0.851
ir_lr <- irf(f2, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 300, ci = "none")
round(apply(ir_lr$estimate, c(1, 2), sum), 3)    # cumulated long-run matrix: upper-right entry is 0
#>         shock
#> response  dinfl unemp
#>    dinfl  0.854 0.000
#>    unemp -3.794 3.949

Cumulative responses. The IRF of a differenced variable is the response of its growth rate; the response of its level is the running sum. cumulative = dinfl cumulates that variable’s response over the horizon, for each draw, before bands are computed:

ir_c <- irf(f2, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 40, ci = "wild", nboot = 300, cumulative = dinfl)
autoplot(ir_c, responses = dinfl)   # level of inflation after the permanent (first) and the transitory shock

The level of inflation converges to a non-zero value after shock 1 (the long-run effect by construction) and returns to zero after shock 2 (restricted to zero, so the bands pinch near zero at long horizons).

I(1) caveats and weak-instrument-like behaviour. If the variables are I(1) and cointegrated, F=I−∑AlF=I-\sum A_l is singular and F−1F^{-1} does not exist: model the cointegrating relations (not possible in this package) or difference the variables, accepting that over-differencing a stationary variable (or a cointegrated pair) corrupts the long-run restriction. With a VAR in levels of a near-integrated system FF is nearly singular, so tiny errors in Âl\hat A_l are amplified in F−1F^{-1}: the long-run multiplier behaves like a ratio with a near-zero denominator, as for a weak instrument. A small simulation (bivariate, true Θ(1)\Theta(1) lower triangular with long-run effect 0.50.5 of shock 1 on variable 2) shows the spread of the estimate rising with persistence ρ\rho:

set.seed(5)
bq_one <- function(rho, n = 200) {
  Fm <- (1 - rho) * diag(2); L <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0, 1), 2); Pm <- Fm %*% L      # Theta(1) = L, lower triangular
  y <- matrix(0, n + 50, 2); for (t in 2:(n + 50)) y[t, ] <- rho * y[t - 1, ] + Pm %*% rnorm(2)
  f <- varm(y[-(1:50), ], p = 1)
  sum(irf(f, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 150, ci = "none")$estimate[2, 1, ])     # estimated long-run effect
}
sapply(c(`rho=0.5` = 0.5, `rho=0.9` = 0.9, `rho=0.97` = 0.97), function(r) { x <- replicate(100, bq_one(r)); c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)) })
#>        rho=0.5   rho=0.9  rho=0.97
#> mean 0.5189669 0.4147380 0.4252881
#> sd   0.2146527 0.4264377 0.6305603

The true value is 0.50.5. The standard deviation grows markedly as ρ→1\rho\to1 (and the estimate acquires finite-sample bias), which is the Faust-Leeper (1997) and Christiano-Eichenbaum-Vigfusson (2006) warning in numbers.

Pitfalls.

  • The restriction is on the long-run multiplier F−1F^{-1}, which is poorly estimated when the VAR is near-integrated (Faust and Leeper, 1997; Christiano, Eichenbaum and Vigfusson, 2006): small errors in ∑lAl\sum_l A_l become large errors in F−1F^{-1}. Check bands; use bias correction (bias_correct = TRUE) or a Bayesian VAR.
  • Whether a variable is modelled in levels or differences changes the identification: over-differencing a stationary variable distorts the restriction.
  • The sign of each column is fixed by the Cholesky factor (positive long-run diagonal), not by economics. Flip signs if you want a “positive supply shock”.

4. Sign restrictions

Definition. Sign restrictions (Faust, 1998; Canova and De Nicolo, 2002; Uhlig, 2005) use Sij(h)∈{−1,0,+1}S_{ij}(h)\in\{-1,0,+1\} and require the IRF of variable ii to shock jj to have sign Sij(h)S_{ij}(h) for h=0,…,Hsh=0,\dots,H_s. Zero entries mean unrestricted. The identified set is 𝒬(B,Σ)={Q:QQ′=I,sign(ei′ΦhP̃Qej)=Sij(h)for all restricted (i,j,h)}. \mathcal{Q}(B,\Sigma)=\Big\{Q:\ QQ'=I,\ \ \mathrm{sign}\big(e_i'\Phi_h\tilde P Q e_j\big)=S_{ij}(h)\ \text{for all restricted }(i,j,h)\Big\} . The algorithm of Rubio-Ramírez, Waggoner and Zha (2010) draws QQ from the Haar (uniform) distribution on the orthogonal group, using the QR decomposition of a Gaussian matrix, and keeps the draw if every column satisfies the restrictions (column sign flips are allowed). For each reduced-form draw, nrot accepted rotations are retained after up to maxtry attempts. In the returned objects the shock dimension is labelled with the variable names whatever the scheme, so with id_sign() index shocks by column position (below: 1 = mp, 2 = demand, 3 = supply). The restrictions are a K×KK\times K matrix (rows: variables, columns: shocks) imposed over horizon periods, or a K×K×HK\times K\times H array. Exact zero restrictions on IRFs (as opposed to unrestricted entries) are not available in id_sign(); combine them with signs in id_zerosign() (section 8).

Economic story. Three shocks distinguished by textbook New-Keynesian signs:

shock inflation unemployment interest rate
monetary-policy −- unrestricted ++
demand ++ −- ++
supply ++ ++ unrestricted

Each is imposed for the first four quarters (impact plus three). The restrictions separate demand from supply by the comovement of inflation and unemployment (a Phillips-curve sign) and the policy shock from demand by the response of inflation. Leaving the unemployment response to monetary policy unrestricted is the Uhlig (2005) “agnostic” approach: the response one most wants to learn about is not imposed.

S <- matrix(0, 3, 3, dimnames = list(colnames(yraw), c("mp", "demand", "supply")))
S["infl", ]  <- c(-1, 1, 1)
S["unemp", ] <- c(0, -1, 1)
S["rate", ]  <- c(1, 1, 0)
S
#>       mp demand supply
#> infl  -1      1      1
#> unemp  0     -1      1
#> rate   1      1      0
id_s <- id_sign(S, horizon = 4, nrot = 1, maxtry = 5000)

Two sources of uncertainty

A set-identified model has two kinds of uncertainty that frequentist or Bayesian bands mix together:

  1. Estimation uncertainty about (B,Σ)(B,\Sigma): the usual sampling or posterior variation.
  2. Identification uncertainty about QQ within 𝒬\mathcal Q: the data cannot say, even in an infinite sample.

Pointwise percentile bands over rotations and reduced-form draws combine them, so wide bands cannot be read as “the data are uninformative”: part of the width is a consequence of the researcher’s choice to leave QQ unrestricted within 𝒬\mathcal Q. Using many rotations at the point estimate isolates identification uncertainty:

# (a) identification uncertainty only: one reduced-form point, many rotations
ir_set <- irf(fit, id = id_sign(S, horizon = 4, nrot = 500, maxtry = 1e5), horizon = 16, ci = "none")
# (b) estimation uncertainty with one rotation per bootstrap draw (mixes both)
ir_mix <- irf(fit, id = id_s, horizon = 16, ci = "bootstrap", nboot = 500)
c(accept_rate_point = ir_set$accept_rate, accept_rate_boot = ir_mix$accept_rate)
#> accept_rate_point  accept_rate_boot 
#>        0.05397237        0.04778744
dim(ir_set$draws)    # [response, shock, horizon, accepted rotations]
#> [1]   3   3  17 500
w <- function(ir, h) {                       # width of the 90% band, unemp response to shock 1 (mp)
  d <- subset(tidy(ir), response == "unemp" & shock == "infl" & level == 0.9 & horizon == h)
  d$conf.high - d$conf.low
}
round(rbind(`rotations only (at point estimate)` = sapply(c(0, 4, 8), w, ir = ir_set),
            `bootstrap + rotations`               = sapply(c(0, 4, 8), w, ir = ir_mix)), 3)
#>                                     [,1]  [,2]  [,3]
#> rotations only (at point estimate) 0.415 0.428 0.170
#> bootstrap + rotations              0.412 0.395 0.205
# shock 1 (mp) is labelled "infl" in the output: shocks carry the variable names
autoplot(ir_mix, shocks = 1) +
  geom_line(data = subset(tidy(ir_set), shock == "infl"), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20")

With a sample of 213 quarters and three variables, the width of the 90% band is almost entirely identification uncertainty: rotating at the point estimate gives bands about as wide as the full bootstrap (the two rows above, for horizons 0, 4 and 8). More data would shrink the second source of uncertainty but not the first.

The solid line and shaded bands are the bootstrap-plus-rotation result; the dashed line is the median of the rotations at the point estimate.

The median is not a model: Fry-Pagan

Pointwise medians across accepted rotations combine IRFs from different rotations Q(n)Q^{(n)}: the median response of unemployment to the “mp” shock may come from one QQ and the median response of inflation from another, so the median path is not the IRF of any single structural model, and responses to different shocks need not be orthogonal. Fry and Pagan (2011) propose the single draw whose IRFs (all variables, shocks and horizons, standardised) are closest to the pointwise median. irf_fry_pagan() extracts the median-target (MT) rotation from the accepted IRFs stored in draws:

mt <- irf_fry_pagan(ir_set)$irf                      # [response, shock, horizon] of the MT draw
mt <- data.frame(subset(tidy(ir_set, bands = FALSE), shock == "infl")[c("response", "horizon")],
                 estimate = as.vector(mt[, 1, ]))
ggplot(subset(tidy(ir_set), shock == "infl" & level == 0.9), aes(horizon, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(aes(y = conf.low), linetype = "dotted", colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = conf.high), linetype = "dotted", colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(1), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = mt, colour = varm_palette(2)[2], linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(vars(response), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Horizon (periods)", y = "Response to the mp shock") + theme_varm()

The orange line is a coherent structural model; the blue line (pointwise median) and the dotted 90% limits summarise the set. Report the MT model when you need one consistent decomposition (a historical decomposition or a counterfactual). hd() with id_sign() uses the first accepted rotation at the point estimate, not the MT rotation, so treat a historical decomposition from a sign identified model as an illustration of one admissible model.

Pitfalls.

  • The prior over QQ is not uninformative about the IRFs: a uniform Haar prior on rotations implies informative priors on the impulse responses (Baumeister and Hamilton, 2015). With few binding restrictions the posterior is largely the prior.
  • accept_rate below a few percent signals that the restrictions are essentially in tension with the data (or too many). A zero acceptance rate stops irf() with an error.
  • Restrictions that hold for many horizons are more informative; impact-only restrictions are the weakest.
  • The identification is only as good as the cross-shock restrictions: without a sign pattern that separates the shocks from each other, the identified shocks are not uniquely labelled.

5. User-supplied impact matrix

id_given(P) accepts any matrix; it does not check PP′=ΣPP'=\Sigma. Use it to reproduce a published impact matrix, or to feed a rotation computed elsewhere (for example from an external routine for zero and sign restrictions).

P <- t(chol(fit$Sigma))
ir_g <- irf(fit, id = id_given(P), horizon = 8, ci = "none")
all.equal(unname(ir_g$estimate[, , 1]), unname(P))
#> [1] TRUE

6. Choosing a scheme and checking it

question cheap check
Is the Cholesky order innocuous? cor(resid(fit)); re-run with another order; overlay a second tidy() on autoplot()
Is there a price puzzle? Sign of the inflation response to the policy shock in the first year
Is the long-run restriction credible? Width of bands at long horizons; compare to bias_correct = TRUE
Do sign restrictions bind? accept_rate; compare the identified-set width to the bootstrap width
Is an FEVD interpretable? fevd() shares are only as good as the identification

7. Zero patterns on impact and long-run responses: id_restrictions()

id_chol() and id_longrun() are two special zero patterns. id_restrictions(impact, longrun) accepts any K×KK\times K matrices with 0 where the impact matrix PP (or the long-run matrix Θ(1)=F−1P\Theta(1)=F^{-1}P) is restricted to zero and NA where it is free. Writing the zeros as ZjZ_j for column jj, the shocks are processed in decreasing order of the number of zeros; the jj-th column qjq_j of the orthogonal matrix QQ is the unit vector in the null space of [ZjL;q1′;…;qj−1′][Z_jL;\,q_1';\dots;q_{j-1}'] (L=chol(Σ)L=\mathrm{chol}(\Sigma)), which exists when the zero counts are K−1,K−2,…,0K-1,K-2,\dots,0 (just-identified). Over-identified patterns are rejected. Each shock is oriented deterministically: the impact response of variable jj to shock jj is positive (or, if that entry is restricted to zero, the first free entry of the column).

Two consistency checks: the lower-triangular pattern reproduces id_chol(), and a lower-triangular long-run pattern reproduces id_longrun().

low <- matrix(NA, 3, 3); low[upper.tri(low)] <- 0
r1 <- irf(fit, id = id_restrictions(impact = low), horizon = 8, ci = "none")
r0 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 8, ci = "none")
max(abs(r1$estimate - r0$estimate))                     # same model
#> [1] 0
lo2 <- matrix(NA, 2, 2); lo2[1, 2] <- 0
r2 <- irf(f2, id = id_restrictions(longrun = lo2), horizon = 100, ci = "none")
max(abs(r2$estimate - irf(f2, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 100, ci = "none")$estimate))
#> [1] 5.551115e-17

Mixed schemes are where it earns its keep. A non-recursive example: in the three-variable system suppose shock 3 moves only the rate on impact (two zeros) and shock 2 does not move the rate (one zero), with shock 1 unrestricted. This is not a permutation of a Cholesky scheme, because variables 1 and 2 respond to each other contemporaneously.

imp <- matrix(c(NA, NA, NA,   NA, NA, 0,   0, 0, NA), 3, dimnames = list(colnames(yraw), paste0("shock", 1:3)))
imp
#>       shock1 shock2 shock3
#> infl      NA     NA      0
#> unemp     NA     NA      0
#> rate      NA      0     NA
ir_ab <- irf(fit, id = id_restrictions(impact = imp), horizon = 8, ci = "none")
round(ir_ab$estimate[, , 1], 3)                         # zeros hold to machine precision
#>         shock
#> response   infl unemp  rate
#>    infl   0.096 0.293 0.000
#>    unemp -0.319 0.092 0.000
#>    rate   0.282 0.000 0.715

Pitfall. Zero restrictions are not testable when the model is just-identified, and an impact zero is a strong claim: it asserts no response within the period. With quarterly data, “no contemporaneous response” is a much stronger assumption than with monthly data.

8. Zero and sign restrictions: id_zerosign() (ARRW)

Pure sign restrictions leave QQ in a large set. Theory often supplies a few exact zeros as well (Arias, Rubio-Ramirez and Waggoner, 2018: ARRW). A zero restriction on the response of variable ii to shock jj at horizon hh reads ei′ΦhLqj=0e_i'\Phi_h L\,q_j=0, a linear constraint on qjq_j.

Algorithm (id_zerosign(), following ARRW Algorithm 2).

  1. Draw a reduced-form (B,Σ)(B,\Sigma) (bootstrap or posterior); set L=chol(Σ)L=\mathrm{chol}(\Sigma).
  2. Order shocks by decreasing number of zeros zjz_j (feasible iff z(j)≤K−jz_{(j)}\le K-j).
  3. For j=1,…,Kj=1,\dots,K: let Nj=[ZjL;q1′;…;qj−1′]N_j=[Z_jL;\,q_1';\dots;q_{j-1}']; draw qjq_j uniformly on the unit sphere of the null space of NjN_j (a Gaussian vector projected on the null space, then normalised).
  4. Form P=LQP=LQ, flip the sign of each column if needed, and keep the draw if all sign restrictions hold. Repeat until nrot rotations are accepted or maxtry is hit.

Zeros hold exactly by construction and PP′=ΣPP'=\Sigma.

Honest caveat: importance weights are not implemented. ARRW show that the draws from this null-space sampler are not uniform on the restricted set, and correct them with a Jacobian weight (a ratio of determinants of A0A_0 and of the volume elements ViV_i). varm does not compute these weights, so accepted draws are unweighted. The output is exact only (i) when there are no zero restrictions (then the sampler is id_sign()), or (ii) when the zeros pin the rotation down up to column signs (then the weights are constant across rotations, although they still vary over reduced-form draws). Under partial zero identification, treat bands as approximate and compare with the pure-sign set.

Example. Make the monetary-policy shock (column 1, as in section 4) have zero impact effect on inflation and unemployment (a recursive-type assumption for that one shock only) while keeping the signs for the others. The impact sign for inflation is dropped for the policy shock since the zero replaces it.

S3 <- array(S, c(3, 3, 4), dimnames = c(dimnames(S), list(NULL)))
S3[1, 1, 1] <- 0                                    # impact inflation response of mp: zero, not a sign
Zm <- matrix(0, 3, 3); Zm[1, 1] <- 1; Zm[2, 1] <- 1 # zero impact on inflation and unemployment, shock 1
id_zs <- id_zerosign(sign = S3, zero = Zm, nrot = 300, maxtry = 1e5)
ir_zs <- irf(fit, id = id_zs, horizon = 16, ci = "none")
ir_zs$accept_rate
#> [1] 0.3792668
round(range(ir_zs$draws[1:2, 1, 1, ]), 12)           # the two impact zeros (all accepted draws)
#> [1] 0 0
ir_s <- irf(fit, id = id_sign(S, horizon = 4, nrot = 300, maxtry = 1e5), horizon = 16, ci = "none")
# shock 1 (mp) is labelled "infl"; ribbon: zero+sign set, dashed: pure-sign median
autoplot(ir_zs, shocks = 1) +
  geom_line(data = subset(tidy(ir_s), shock == "infl"), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20")

The solid line (with its ribbons) is the median of the zero-plus-sign set and the dashed line the pure-sign median. Compare the two sets: the zeros remove the rotations that violate them. Because the zero restriction is not conjugate, the posterior mass within this set is the approximate piece (above). For a fully-identified zero pattern, id_restrictions() is exact.

Long-run zeros are available through zero_lr (a K×KK\times K 0/1 matrix, 1 = cumulative response is zero), e.g. a demand shock with no long-run effect on a level; the counting rule is the same, and the same near-unit-root pitfalls as section 3 apply.

9. A data-generating process with known truth

To see which methods recover the truth we need a DGP whose structural impact matrix is known. Take K=3K=3, yt=A1yt−1+Pεty_t=A_1y_{t-1}+P\varepsilon_t with unit-variance shocks and

P=(10.60−0.4100.501),A1=(0.50.100.10.40.100.10.3). P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.6&0\\-0.4&1&0\\0.5&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad A_1=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.1&0\\0.1&0.4&0.1\\0&0.1&0.3\end{pmatrix}.

The target is shock 1 (column 1 of PP), normalised to move y1y_1 by one unit on impact. Features: (i) PP has P12=0.6≠0P_{12}=0.6\ne0, so y1y_1 responds contemporaneously to shock 2 and the recursive ordering (y1,y2,y3)(y_1,y_2,y_3) is wrong; (ii) PP has three zeros (P13,P23,P32P_{13},P_{23},P_{32}) in a non-recursive pattern that id_restrictions() can exploit; (iii) an instrument zt=ε1t+νtz_t=\varepsilon_{1t}+\nu_t is available.

P0 <- matrix(c(1, -0.4, 0.5,   0.6, 1, 0,   0, 0, 1), 3)
A1 <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.1, 0,   0.1, 0.4, 0.1,   0, 0.1, 0.3), 3)
simvar <- function(n, sdv = NULL, burn = 100) {
  eps <- matrix(rnorm((n + burn) * 3), ncol = 3)
  if (!is.null(sdv)) eps[burn + seq_len(n), ] <- eps[burn + seq_len(n), ] * sdv   # sdv: n x 3 shock sd's
  y <- matrix(0, n + burn, 3)
  for (t in 2:(n + burn)) y[t, ] <- A1 %*% y[t - 1, ] + P0 %*% eps[t, ]
  list(y = `colnames<-`(y[-seq_len(burn), ], c("y1", "y2", "y3")), eps = eps[-seq_len(burn), ])
}
truth <- function(H) {                                  # response of (y1,y2,y3) to shock 1, y1 impact = 1
  Ph <- diag(3); out <- matrix(0, 3, H + 1)
  for (h in 0:H) { out[, h + 1] <- Ph %*% P0[, 1]; Ph <- A1 %*% Ph }
  out / out[1, 1]
}
set.seed(7)
sm <- simvar(400)
fs <- varm(sm$y, p = 1)
tr <- truth(12)
round(tr[, 1:4], 2)
#>      [,1]  [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]  1.0  0.46 0.23 0.12
#> [2,] -0.4 -0.01 0.05 0.05
#> [3,]  0.5  0.11 0.03 0.01

Now identify shock 1 four ways, from the same sample, and compare to the truth (black).

one <- normalise_to(y1, y1, 1)                           # impact on y1 = 1
z <- sm$eps[, 1] + rnorm(400, sd = 0.7)                  # strong instrument
Ssim <- matrix(0, 3, 3, dimnames = list(colnames(sm$y), paste0("s", 1:3))); Ssim[, 1] <- c(1, -1, 1)
ir_ch <- irf(fs, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, ci = "none", normalise = one)
ir_ab <- irf(fs, id = id_restrictions(impact = imp), horizon = 12, ci = "none", normalise = one)
ir_px <- irf(fs, id = id_proxy(z, fs, target = y1, size = 1), horizon = 12, ci = "none")
ir_sg <- irf(fs, id = id_sign(Ssim, horizon = 1, nrot = 400, maxtry = 1e5), horizon = 12, ci = "none",
             normalise = one)
td_sg <- tidy(ir_sg, bands = FALSE)
td_sg$estimate <- as.vector(irf_fry_pagan(ir_sg)$irf)    # the median-target draw instead of the pointwise median
td_tr <- tidy(ir_ch, bands = FALSE)                       # same layout, filled with the truth
td_tr$estimate <- 0
td_tr$estimate[td_tr$shock == "y1"] <- as.vector(tr)      # shock-1 truth, ordered response within horizon
stacked <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(d, m) cbind(d[d$shock == "y1", ], method = m),
  list(td_tr, tidy(ir_ch, bands = FALSE), tidy(ir_ab, bands = FALSE), tidy(ir_px, bands = FALSE), td_sg),
  c("truth", "Cholesky", "restrictions", "proxy", "sign (MT)")))
stacked$method <- factor(stacked$method, c("truth", "Cholesky", "restrictions", "proxy", "sign (MT)"))
ggplot(stacked, aes(horizon, estimate, colour = method, linetype = method, linewidth = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", varm_palette(5)[c(5, 3, 1, 2)]), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", rep("dashed", 4)), name = NULL) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(1.4, rep(0.8, 4)), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(vars(response), scales = "free_y", labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Horizon (periods)", y = "Response to shock 1 (impact on y1 = 1)") + theme_varm()

Cholesky is biased because its ordering assumption is false; the zero-restriction scheme (which encodes the true pattern) and the proxy track the truth. The sign-identified median target model lies within the identified set but is not guaranteed to be close: signs alone are weak. Impact errors across one hundred samples quantify this:

set.seed(11)
mc <- t(replicate(100, {
  s <- simvar(300); f <- varm(s$y, p = 1); zz <- s$eps[, 1] + rnorm(300, sd = 0.7)
  c(chol = irf(f, id = id_chol(), horizon = 1, ci = "none", normalise = one)$estimate["y2", "y1", 1],
    restr = irf(f, id = id_restrictions(impact = imp), horizon = 1, ci = "none", normalise = one)$estimate["y2", "y1", 1],
    proxy = irf(f, id = id_proxy(zz, f, target = y1), horizon = 1, ci = "none")$estimate["y2", "y1", 1])
}))
rbind(mean = colMeans(mc), sd = apply(mc, 2, sd), rmse = sqrt(colMeans((mc + 0.4)^2)))   # truth: impact of shock 1 on y2 = -0.4
#>            chol      restr       proxy
#> mean 0.14332574 -0.4292148 -0.40800481
#> sd   0.05725749  0.2125344  0.09789596
#> rmse 0.54630440  0.2134776  0.09773361

The Cholesky mean misses −0.4-0.4 (a bias that does not vanish with TT), whereas the other two are centred on it. The proxy is the most precise here because the instrument is strong (reliability about 0.7); the zero scheme is correct but noisier, since the three zeros identify the direction of shock 1 only through the estimated Σ\Sigma. A weak instrument would reverse the ranking (see below).

10. External instruments (proxy SVAR)

Set-up. Let ztz_t be a scalar external instrument for shock ε1t\varepsilon_{1t} and write ut=sε1t+…u_t=s\,\varepsilon_{1t}+\dots with ss the impact vector. Mertens and Ravn (2013) and Stock and Watson (2018) require

  • relevance: E[ztε1t]=ϕ≠0E[z_t\varepsilon_{1t}]=\phi\ne0;
  • exogeneity (contemporaneous): E[ztεjt]=0E[z_t\varepsilon_{jt}]=0 for j>1j>1.

Then γ=E[utzt]=sϕ\gamma=E[u_tz_t]=s\phi, so s∝γs\propto\gamma, identified up to scale. id_proxy() estimates γ̂=T−1∑ûtzt\hat\gamma=T^{-1}\sum\hat u_tz_t and scales it so that variable target moves by size on impact, s=size⋅γ̂/γ̂targets=\text{size}\cdot\hat\gamma/\hat\gamma_{target}; the IRF is Φhs\Phi_hs. Only column shock of the IRF array (default: the position of target) is identified: the other columns are zero, so FEVD of other shocks is meaningless, and the FEVD of the proxy shock is only right if size equals the shock standard deviation, which a proxy cannot deliver.

Relevance. The first stage is the regression of the target residual on ztz_t. proxy_fstat() reports F (classical), F_robust (HC1) and F_hac, the Montiel Olea, Stock and Watson (2021) Wald statistic that accounts for estimation of the VAR coefficients and serial correlation; F_hac is what matters for the robust intervals. Rules of thumb: below about 10 the normalised IRF γ̂i/γ̂target\hat\gamma_i/\hat\gamma_{target} is a ratio with a denominator near zero: it has fat tails, is not normal, and bootstrap percentile bands undercover.

z_weak <- 0.08 * sm$eps[, 1] + rnorm(400)                # nearly irrelevant instrument
rbind(strong = proxy_fstat(fs, z, "y1"), weak = proxy_fstat(fs, z_weak, "y1"))
#>                  F    F_robust       F_hac
#> strong 433.2734693 390.9114603 186.2869674
#> weak     0.2847472   0.2635655   0.2361444

Inference. irf(fit, id_proxy(z, fit), ci = ...) redraws (B,Σ)(B,\Sigma) but holds γ\gamma fixed, so it understates uncertainty; use proxy_draws(), which carries one γ*\gamma^* per draw. It offers two bootstraps:

  • "wild": a common Rademacher weight wtw_t multiplies (ût,zt)(\hat u_t,z_t). Since wt2=1w_t^2=1, T−1∑(wtût)(wtzt)=γ̂T^{-1}\sum (w_t\hat u_t)(w_tz_t)=\hat\gammaexactly: the key moment is not resampled at all, and γ*\gamma^* varies only through the re-estimated VAR coefficients. This is why Jentsch and Lunsford (2019, 2022) show the wild bootstrap is invalid for proxy SVARs, with bands far too narrow.
  • "mbb" (default): moving-block bootstrap of the pairs (ût,zt)(\hat u_t,z_t), which preserves their joint serial dependence and does resample the moment γ̂\hat\gamma; valid under strong instruments. The block length defaults to the Jentsch-Lunsford rule round(5.03T1/4)\mathrm{round}(5.03\,T^{1/4}), the same rule as varm_proxy().

In the package’s Monte Carlo (validation/proxy-coverage.R and validation/ident-extra.R, not run here) the nominal 90% band for the impact response of a non-target variable covered the truth only 13.5% of the time with a strong instrument and 21% with a weak one (and 15% in ident-extra.R) under the wild bootstrap, versus 87% for the moving-block bootstrap with a strong instrument. Band widths on one simulated sample show the same thing:

pb_w <- proxy_draws(fs, z, nboot = 300, type = "wild", target = y1)
pb_m <- proxy_draws(fs, z, nboot = 300, type = "mbb", target = y1)
ir_w <- irf(pb_w$draws, pb_w$id, horizon = 12)
ir_m <- irf(pb_m$draws, pb_m$id, horizon = 12)
both <- rbind(cbind(tidy(ir_m), method = "mbb"), cbind(tidy(ir_w), method = "wild"))
both <- subset(both, shock == "y1" & level == 0.9)
both$width <- both$conf.high - both$conf.low
round(with(subset(both, response == "y2" & horizon %in% c(0, 2, 4)), tapply(width, list(method, horizon), c)), 3)   # 90% width, y2
#>          0     2     4
#> mbb  0.181 0.109 0.052
#> wild 0.022 0.114 0.058
subset(both, response == "y2" & horizon == 0)[c("method", "conf.low", "conf.high")]   # truth: -0.4
#>     method   conf.low  conf.high
#> 2      mbb -0.4205651 -0.2400096
#> 236   wild -0.3161437 -0.2940591
ggplot(both, aes(horizon, estimate, colour = method, fill = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = varm_palette(2)) + scale_fill_manual(values = varm_palette(2)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(response), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Horizon (periods)", y = "Response to shock 1 (proxy)") + theme_varm()

At impact, where the normalisation divides by γ̂target\hat\gamma_{target} and the key moment matters, the wild-bootstrap band is roughly an order of magnitude narrower than the block-bootstrap band and here excludes the true value −0.4-0.4 (table and intervals above). At later horizons the two widths are close, because the re-estimated VAR coefficients dominate. The same results are available in one call with varm_proxy(fit, m, method = "mbb"), which also reports the shock series and the instrument reliability.

vp <- varm_proxy(fs, m = z, target = "y1", horizon = 8, nboot = 200)
vp
#> <varm_proxy> shock to y1 (size 1), horizon 0..8, 200 moving-block-bootstrap draws (block length 22)
#> first-stage F = 433.3; robust F = 390.9
#> instrument reliability: 0.657
round(vp$estimate[1:3, ], 3)
#>      y1     y2    y3
#> 0 1.000 -0.307 0.533
#> 1 0.467  0.072 0.176
#> 2 0.242  0.110 0.074

Weak-instrument-robust sets. varm_proxy_robust() implements the Montiel Olea, Stock and Watson (2021) Anderson-Rubin-type confidence sets. For each response λ\lambda it inverts the HAC Wald test of sei′ΦhΓ−λΓtarget=0s\,e_i'\Phi_h\Gamma-\lambda\Gamma_{target}=0; the set is one of a bounded interval, the complement of an interval, empty, or the whole real line. With a strong instrument it is a normal-looking interval; with a weak one the honest answer is “the data cannot tell”: the set is unbounded.

rb_s <- varm_proxy_robust(fs, m = z, target = "y1", horizon = 4, level = 0.90)
rb_w <- varm_proxy_robust(fs, m = z_weak, target = "y1", horizon = 4, level = 0.90)
rbind(strong = c(rb_s$lower[1, "y2", 1], rb_s$upper[1, "y2", 1], rb_s$case[1, "y2", 1]),
      weak   = c(rb_w$lower[1, "y2", 1], rb_w$upper[1, "y2", 1], rb_w$case[1, "y2", 1]))   # lower, upper, case (1 bounded, 2 complement, 4 real line)
#>              [,1]       [,2] [,3]
#> strong -0.4091685 -0.2099833    1
#> weak         -Inf        Inf    4

(The columns are the 90% lower limit, upper limit and set type for the impact response of y2y_2; the truth is −0.4-0.4.)

Pitfalls. (i) The proxy must be uncorrelated with all other structural shocks, not merely with the policy rule; high-frequency surprises can contain an information effect. (ii) If the proxy sample is shorter than the VAR, missing values must be 0-filled only when the instrument is truly zero there; NAs are rejected. (iii) A single instrument identifies one shock; with rr instruments varm_proxy(target = c(...)) identifies rr shocks up to a Cholesky-type restriction within the target block, so the order of target matters. (iv) varm_proxy_bayes() gives a posterior alternative (see its help).

10.1 Full-posterior and robust-Bayes proxy-SVARs

varm_proxy_bayes() is limited-information: the proxy never touches (B,Σ)(B,\Sigma) and nothing restricts the shock. Two functions add the missing machinery, both built on a [bvarm()] fit (so the reduced-form prior is whatever you chose, e.g. Minnesota) and on a first-stage regression of the proxy, mt=Dyt+Gxt+∑lHlmt−l+vtm_t=Dy_t+Gx_t+\sum_l H_lm_{t-l}+v_t, with a Jeffreys prior. Writing Σ=ΣtrΣtr′\Sigma=\Sigma_{tr}\Sigma_{tr}' and yt=Bxt+ΣtrQεty_t=Bx_t+\Sigma_{tr}Q\varepsilon_t, the proxy covariances are E[mtεt′]=DΣtrQE[m_t\varepsilon_t']=D\Sigma_{tr}Q, so exogeneity (mm uncorrelated with the first K−rK-r shocks) is a set of linear restrictions on the columns of QQ. Convention: the r proxies are correlated with the last r shocks.

  • varm_proxy_arw() / id_proxy_bayes() (Arias, Rubio-Ramirez and Waggoner 2021 type): exact independent posterior draws, adding sign restrictions on the proxy shocks, a reliability truncation, and lags of yy and mm in the proxy equation. With one proxy the shock is point-identified; with several, exogeneity leaves an orthogonal rotation of the proxy shocks that only signs pin down. The draws plug into irf().
  • varm_proxy_gkr() (Giacomini, Kitagawa and Read 2022): for set-identified shocks, instead of one arbitrary prior on the unrevisable rotation, report the set of posterior means and the robust credible region over all priors on the admissible rotations (GKR Algorithm 2, with draws of QQ instead of a numerical optimiser).
bf <- bvarm(sm$y, p = 1, ndraw = 400, nburn = 200)
arw <- varm_proxy_arw(bf, z, target = "y1", horizon = 8)
round(rbind(truth = tr[, 1], posterior_median = arw$estimate[1, ], lo90 = arw$bands[1, , 1], hi90 = arw$bands[1, , 4]), 2)
#>                  y1    y2   y3
#> truth             1 -0.40 0.50
#> posterior_median  1 -0.31 0.53
#> lo90              1 -0.43 0.43
#> hi90              1 -0.21 0.63
ir_arw <- irf(bf, id_proxy_bayes(bf, z, target = "y1"), horizon = 8)   # same draws through irf()

The same DGP in the robust-Bayes setting. In the GKR ordering the true shock 2 (PP’s second column, (0.6,1,0)′(0.6,1,0)') is one of the two non-proxy shocks, which exogeneity alone cannot tell apart. With the sign restriction “shock 1 raises y1y_1 and y2y_2 on impact” its impact response is only set-identified:

S <- matrix(0, 3, 3); S[1:2, 1] <- 1
gk <- varm_proxy_gkr(bf, z, signs = S, shock = 1, horizon = 4, nq = 100)
rbind(set_of_means_lower = gk$lower[1, ], set_of_means_upper = gk$upper[1, ],
      robust_90_lo = gk$region[1, , 1], robust_90_hi = gk$region[1, , 4],
      single_prior_median = gk$estimate[1, ])
#>                               y1           y2         y3
#> set_of_means_lower  1.599107e-02 8.549768e-02 -1.0057139
#> set_of_means_upper  5.374786e-01 9.499538e-01  0.5700843
#> robust_90_lo        2.971019e-05 1.490977e-06 -1.0703288
#> robust_90_hi        5.928206e-01 9.981810e-01  0.7096259
#> single_prior_median 4.474327e-01 8.189190e-01 -0.3899005
gk$prob_nonempty
#> [1] 1

The two non-proxy shocks are only identified up to a rotation in the 2-dimensional space orthogonal to the proxy direction, so the set of means is wide, whereas the single-prior (Haar) posterior reports one narrower number that depends on the prior. GKR recommend reporting both. The true shock 2, (0.6,1,0)′(0.6, 1, 0)', satisfies the signs but sits at the upper edge of the identified set (it is nearly the most extreme admissible rotation), so its y2y_2 impact (1) lies slightly above the estimated set of means; the 90% robust region extends to it on y1y_1 and nearly on y2y_2. Averaging bounds over draws and approximating the set by random rotations both err on the narrow side at such boundary points. The approximation of the identified set by random rotations underestimates it at each draw and converges as nq grows; strong proxies are assumed (GKR sec. 3).

What is not implemented. Caldara and Herbst’s (2019) Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler with a structural measurement equation and priors on (β,σν)(\beta,\sigma_\nu); the ARW structural-prior importance weights (volume element); and GKR’s constrained-optimiser Algorithm 1.

11. Identification through heteroskedasticity

If the covariance changes across two known regimes, Σ1=PP′\Sigma_1=PP' and Σ2=PΛP′\Sigma_2=P\Lambda P' with Λ=diag(λ1,…,λK)\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_K) distinct, then PP is identified (Rigobon, 2003) up to column order and sign, without any economic restriction. With Σ1=L1L1′\Sigma_1=L_1L_1', take the eigendecomposition L1−1Σ2L1−′=VΛV′L_1^{-1}\Sigma_2L_1^{-\prime}=V\Lambda V' and set P=L1VP=L_1V. id_hetero(fit, regime) implements it with shocks ordered by decreasing λj\lambda_j (relative variance in regime 2) and signs set so that diag(P)>0\mathrm{diag}(P)>0. It returns an id_given() object with the eigenvalues as attribute lambda.

set.seed(21)
nn <- 600; reg <- rep(0:1, each = nn / 2)
sdv <- cbind(ifelse(reg == 1, 2, 1), 1, ifelse(reg == 1, 0.5, 1))     # variance ratios 4, 1, 0.25
sh <- simvar(nn, sdv = sdv)
fh <- varm(sh$y, p = 1)
idh <- id_hetero(fh, regime = reg)
round(attr(idh, "lambda"), 2)                                          # true: 4, 1, 0.25
#> [1] 4.00 0.84 0.23
round(cbind(true = P0[, 1] / P0[1, 1], est = idh$P[, 1] / idh$P[1, 1]), 2)   # shock 1, y1 impact = 1
#>    true   est
#> y1  1.0  1.00
#> y2 -0.4 -0.39
#> y3  0.5  0.50

The estimated λ\lambda and the first column recover the truth up to sampling error. Limits to keep in mind:

  • This is a point estimate only: idh is an id_given() with a fixed PP, so irf(fit, idh, ci = "bootstrap") resamples (B,Σ)(B,\Sigma) but not PP and understates uncertainty.
  • Identification needs distinct λj\lambda_j; near-equal ratios mean a near-singular eigenproblem and unstable columns (a weak-identification problem).
  • The regimes must be known (or estimated elsewhere) and PP constant across them.
  • Shocks are statistical, ordered by volatility change; labelling them economically is a separate, untested step.

12. Why sign-identified bands are not like other bands, and a labelling pitfall

Sign restrictions share two pitfalls worth stating in one place.

Shocks are indexed by position, not by name. The shock dimension of the returned IRF array carries the variable names (colnames(yraw)) whatever the scheme. With id_sign()/id_zerosign()/id_restrictions() shock jj is column jj of the restriction matrix, so label the shocks yourself ("mp", "demand", "supply" in section 4) and index by position. Dimnames of the restriction matrix are ignored by irf().

Bands mix model and identification uncertainty. Pointwise percentile bands over (reduced-form draws ×\times rotations) combine estimation uncertainty with the width of the identified set. Extra data narrows only the first. A defensible report shows both: the set at the point estimate (many rotations, ci = "none") and the full band, as in section 4, together with the Fry-Pagan model:

fp <- irf_fry_pagan(ir_set)                     # ir_set: rotations at the point estimate (section 4)
fp$index; fp$varm_draw                          # which accepted draw; which reduced-form draw it came from
#> [1] 77
#> [1] 1
round(fp$impact, 3)                             # its impact matrix (response x shock)
#>         shock
#> response   infl  unemp  rate
#>    infl  -0.156  0.192 0.183
#>    unemp -0.096 -0.265 0.176
#>    rate   0.614  0.331 0.323

irf_fry_pagan() returns a coherent structural model (an IRF array, its impact matrix, and the indexes of the draw), unlike the pointwise median, so shocks from it can be used for historical decompositions and counterfactuals. It depends on the prior over rotations and is a summary of the set, not an estimate.

13. Which identification for which question?

shock typical question credible identifications in varm main threat
Monetary policy effect of a rate surprise on inflation and unemployment id_proxy() with high-frequency or narrative surprises (best when an instrument exists); id_chol() with policy last in a rich system; id_sign()/id_zerosign() with price-puzzle-avoiding signs information effects and weak instruments (proxy); omitted forward-looking variables (Cholesky, price puzzle); prior-driven bands (signs)
Fiscal multiplier of a spending or tax change id_chol() with government spending ordered first (Blanchard-Perotti-style timing, no discretionary response within the quarter); id_proxy() with narrative tax or spending news; id_restrictions() with an external elasticity in AA anticipation (fiscal foresight makes the VAR non-invertible); timing assumptions at low frequency
Oil effect of oil price changes on activity and inflation id_sign()/id_zerosign() separating supply, aggregate demand and oil-specific demand by comovements; id_proxy() with oil-supply news; id_chol() with oil first composition (the demand origin of oil price changes); sign-set width; labelled shocks are not unique
Technology effect of a productivity shock on hours and output id_longrun() / id_restrictions(longrun = ) (Gali, Blanchard-Quah); id_proxy() with utilisation-adjusted TFP near-unit-root persistence (poor long-run estimate), over-differencing, level vs. difference specification
No economic prior, volatility shifts statistical shocks, then labelled id_hetero() weak identification, regimes must be known, point estimate only

General guidance. (1) If you have a plausible instrument, prefer id_proxy(); it needs the weakest assumptions about the rest of the system but gives only one shock. (2) Use signs when theory speaks only about co-movement, and report the identified set and the Fry-Pagan model. (3) Add exact zeros (id_zerosign(), id_restrictions()) only for things you would defend as exact. (4) Check robustness across schemes: if the answer is the same under Cholesky, signs and a proxy, the identification is not doing the work.
